etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Latin candidātus (“a person who is standing for public office”), from candidus (“dazzling white, shining, clear”) +‎ -ātus, -āta, -ātum (participial adjective-forming suffix), in reference to Roman candidates wearing bleached white togas as a symbol of purity at a public forum. Equivalent to candid +‎ -ate (noun-forming suffix).

definitions.definition: A person who is running in an election.
A person who is applying for a job.
Something or somebody that may be suitable.

quote.citation: 2013 May-June, Kevin Heng, “Why Does Nature Form Exoplanets Easily?”, in American Scientist, volume 101, number 3, page 184:
quote.text: In the past two years, NASA’s Kepler Space Telescope has located nearly 3,000 exoplanet candidates ranging from sub-Earth-sized minions to gas giants that dwarf our own Jupiter.

definitions.definition: (genetics) A gene which may play a role in a given disease.
(uncommon) To stand as a candidate for an office, especially a religious one.

quote.citation: 1906, Year Book of the Central Conference of American Rabbis, page 196:
quote.text: The matter of candidating for a pulpit is not a matter of difference between congregations and Rabbis, but between Rabbis themselves.

quote.citation: 1917, William Harvey Allen, Universal Training for Citizenship and Public Service, page 154:
quote.text: Furthermore, the fact that a school principal has only been in a large school six weeks does not prevent his candidating for principal of a larger school with larger salary.

quote.citation: 2014, Susan H. Jones, Listening for God's Call, SCM Press, →ISBN, page 74:
quote.text: The report Shaping the Future also gives a set of learning outcomes for those people candidating for ordained ministry. These were also agreed by the Methodist Conference.

definitions.definition: (nonstandard, chiefly in jargon and non-native speakers' English) To make or name (something) a candidate (for use, for study as a next project, for investigation as a possible cause of something, etc).
